Mit einer Illustration wurde bekannt, dass der Manga »Phantom Busters« von Neoshoco eine Anime-Adaption erhält und soll im Laufe des nächsten Jahres 2027 im japanischen TV starten. Weitere Informationen zur Produktionteam und Sprechercast sind zum aktuellen Zeitpunkt noch nicht bekannt.

Die Reihe startete in Japan im August 2023 im Jump SQ Magazin von Shueisha und umfasst bislang sieben Bände. Das achte Band erscheint am 2. Oktober in Japan. Eine englische Veröffentlichung erscheint bei VIZ Media (4 Bände), während hierzulande die Reihe bei Carlsen Manga (2 Bände) auf Deutsch erhältlich ist.

📜 Beschreibung 》
Der Musterschüler Eugene Korekishi glaubt nicht an Geister, bis er auf Mogari Shishikuno trifft. Dieser ist ein Exorzist mit einer ziemlich ungewöhnlichen Methode: Statt Geister zu bekämpfen, verschlingt er sie einfach. Da Mogari die Geister selbst jedoch nicht sehen kann, braucht er Menschen mit besonderer Wahrnehmung an seiner Seite. Gemeinsam gründen sie an ihrer Schule einen Exorzisten-Club, der schon bald nach einem vierten Mitglied sucht und dabei auf Kotaro Tamon stößt, einen Jungen, der mit Geistern sprechen kann, aber kaum mit seinen lebenden Mitschülern.

record.text: Microsoft relaunched Copilot with Home, Code and Autopilot. It looks a lot like Claude, but the real story is distribution: Microsoft is already inside the business.

external.description:
Microsoft relaunched Copilot on Friday, and my first reaction was that it looks as though they've copied Claude. There's a Home tab where Chat and Cowork live side by side, a Code tab where you build apps by describing them, and an Autopilot tab for an agent that keeps working when you don't. If you've spent the last year in Claude or ChatGPT, you'll recognise every screen.

I read the announcement, watched Microsoft's launch video and recorded my take. Here's where I land, and why I think the resemblance is the least interesting part of the story.

### What Microsoft actually launched

In Microsoft's own words, the new Copilot has three parts. **Home** is the starting point where Chat and Cowork come together, with Word, Excel and PowerPoint built right into Copilot. **Code** lets non-developers build dashboards, workflows and internal apps in plain language, on the same technology as GitHub Copilot. **Autopilot** is a persistent agent with its own identity, memory and workspace inside your tenant, and you reach it with an @mention in Teams or Outlook.

Home and Code roll out to Microsoft's Frontier program first, and Autopilot goes to private preview at the end of the month. The agentic parts are billed on usage rather than a flat seat price.

### Yes, it looks like Claude

The resemblance isn't a coincidence. Earlier this year Microsoft said it was bringing the technology platform that powers Claude Cowork into Microsoft 365 Copilot. And Microsoft's Copilot chief Jacob Andreou acknowledged to CNBC that adding coding to the app is Microsoft playing catch-up.

I don't see that as a weakness. It's a very Microsoft move: arrive later than the market, rebuild what everyone else already built, and make it feel native to the tools people use all day. Anyone who has been trying Claude or ChatGPT over the last year now finds the same patterns inside the suite their company already pays for. The learning curve will be short.

One thing I'd still change. Microsoft keeps Chat, Cowork and Autopilot as separate modes, and you have to switch between them. I'm still looking for the one tool that takes whatever I type and works out on its own whether it's a quick question, a job for Cowork or a routine for my assistant. I wrote about that same friction when Claude merged Chat and Cowork, and the line between chat and agent is still the hardest part of these products to get right.

### Autopilot is the part I'd watch

Of the three, Autopilot is the one that excites me most. It's an assistant that works on your behalf even when your laptop is closed: the weekly report, the monthly review, the follow-up nobody remembers to send. Microsoft's own example is running a supplier review.

That example says a lot. It's not a writing prompt or a coding demo. It's procurement, the kind of process that runs through the middle of real businesses.

### The moat isn't the product

This is where Microsoft is far ahead of everyone else. They are already inside the business. They sit in supply chains, in procurement, in finance, in the email and calendars of most large companies. Try convincing a company that runs on the Microsoft suite to move everything to Anthropic or to OpenAI. That's a hard sell, no matter how good the other product is.

And there's the part people underestimate: Microsoft's sales force. Its account managers already own the relationship with these companies and can position Copilot as a core product that plugs into their systems. It's the same logic I wrote about in why a me-too product can still win if you already own the customer.

The opportunity is large. According to CNBC, fewer than 7% of Microsoft's 450 million commercial Office 365 seats pay for Copilot today. That's not a product problem you solve with features. It's an adoption problem, and adoption is exactly where Microsoft's reach does the work.

> As Tim Brown puts it in _Change by Design_ : new products may be doomed for all sorts of reasons, from uneven quality and unimaginative marketing to unreliable distribution or unrealistic pricing.

Microsoft has the distribution covered. What decides this launch is the rest of that list.

### The organisational work nobody mentions

Rolling this out in a large company isn't a licence switch. Code gives everyone the power to build their own tools. That's great until you have thousands of people building little apps across the business, each on whatever data they happen to have access to. Without training and clear ownership, you get a sprawl of tools that nobody maintains and numbers that don't match. I've seen the lighter version of this with documents already: polished AI output that shifts the work onto whoever opens it.

This is where experience matters more than the tool. The companies that get value out of Code and Autopilot will be the ones where someone with real domain knowledge decides what gets automated, on which data, and who owns it. The tool makes building cheap. It doesn't make judgement cheap.

### Would I switch?

Not anytime soon. I haven't tried the new Copilot yet, and that's the big caveat on everything above. I work on the Google suite, my business runs on Claude, and Claude already works well with PowerPoint and Excel. Switching would be a steep move for me.

But I'm not the target customer. For the many companies already running on Microsoft, this could be a real game changer. Microsoft rarely ships something half done, and if they execute well, they have a winner on their hands.

The product looks like Claude. The distribution doesn't look like anyone else's.

record.text: Thirty short FAQ posts sat in Search Console as crawled-not-indexed. Here is how I rebuilt the cluster around the questions people actually type, used Google's own image filter chips as the entity checklist, and consolidated with canonical tags instead of deleting anything.

external.description:
My own site had a page whose entire job was to link to other pages. Twenty-eight of them, in a bare list, under a heading that promised to explain hiring a fractional executive. Underneath it sat roughly thirty short posts, most answering a single question in a few hundred words, most of them sitting in Search Console as "crawled — currently not indexed".

That is not a problem you fix by writing more posts. It is a shape problem. Google had looked at the cluster and decided it wasn't worth keeping, and honestly, it was right.

Last week I rebuilt the whole thing. I also used the rebuild to test a technique on something I own, before I let it anywhere near a client's site.

### Let the search results tell you the headings

The technique is two steps and costs nothing but attention. First: take the People Also Ask questions Google shows for your target query and use those as your H2s — the literal question, in the literal phrasing people type, not your internal way of naming the topic. Second: search each of those questions, switch to the Images tab, and read the filter chips along the top. Those chips are the entities Google associates with that exact question. Weave them into the answer that sits under that heading.

It is a cheap, observable proxy for a slice of Google's entity graph, per question rather than per topic. You are not guessing which related concepts belong in a section. You are being shown them.

For my cluster I ran six queries through it — what a fractional executive is, what one costs, fractional versus interim, when to hire, what they actually do, how to choose. The consolidated entity set that came back was blunt and useful: fractional CFO, CMO, COO, CTO, C-suite, interim leadership, executive search, retainer, executive compensation, company size. Half of those I would have written anyway. The other half I would have left out because they felt too obvious to bother with, which is exactly the instinct that gets you a page nobody finds.

> As Renée Mauborgne writes in _Blue Ocean Shift_ , companies "define the scope of their offering as the industry has long defined it." The same trap sits in your headings. You describe the work the way your industry describes it, and your buyer types something else entirely.

### Canonicals, not a graveyard

The rebuild turned that 28-item link list into thirteen question-shaped sections, each one folding in the substance of the thin posts it replaced, each carrying the entities for its own question. Twenty-nine internal links now sit inside prose instead of in a pile.

The part I want to flag is what happened to the old posts. I did not delete them and I did not unpublish them. Twenty of them got a `canonical_url` pointing at the hub. They stay live, they still resolve, and Google is told plainly which URL is the one that matters. Google's own guidance on consolidating duplicate URLs treats this as the normal move, and it has two properties I like: zero 404 risk, and it is reversible on an afternoon's notice if the measurement says I was wrong.

Deleting would have been faster and it would have felt more decisive. It also would have been irreversible, which is a bad trade for a change whose effect I cannot see for six weeks. I have written before about the work being in what you decide not to index — this is the same call from the other direction.

### The schema part, honestly

I regenerated the FAQPage JSON-LD to match the twelve on-page question-and-answer pairs, and I want to be precise about why, because there is a lot of stale advice here. Google cut FAQ rich results back to a small set of authoritative sites in August 2023 and has narrowed them since. If you are adding FAQ markup for the star-and-accordion look in the results page, you are working from a 2022 playbook.

I still ship it, for a different reason. The markup is an unambiguous machine-readable statement of "this page answers this question with this answer", and the things reading pages now are not only the blue-links index. Expect nothing in the SERP and you will not be disappointed; the structure is doing its work elsewhere.

What actually earns the ranking is the same thing it has always been: a page that answers the question better than the alternatives, which is all Google's helpful content guidance has ever asked for. The entity chips don't replace that. They stop you writing a good answer that omits the three concepts the reader assumed you would cover.

### Where I will not use it

I rolled the same technique into two other properties the same day — a set of service pages that hadn't been written yet, which is the cheapest possible moment to apply it, and ninety-seven town pages in a directory, where it went into the generator rather than the pages, so it survives the domain migration that project is heading for.

I am not putting it into the essays. Not these ones. The house voice here is the asset, and retrofitting an honest field note into a question-and-answer layout would strip the one thing that makes it worth reading. Query augmentation belongs on surfaces that are already structured: hubs, reference pages, service pages, FAQ blocks. It does not belong anywhere someone is reading for the argument. The same discipline applies to any tool that promises reach — the leverage is in knowing where it does and doesn't apply, not in applying it everywhere.

Measurement is the honest part of this post that I can't give you yet. The baseline is thirty posts largely not indexed and a hub ranking for almost nothing. In four to six weeks I check one number: how many distinct queries the hub URL picks up, and whether the folded URLs drop out as the canonicals are honoured. If it doesn't move, I'll say so here.

Either way, I stopped writing the headings I wanted to write and started writing the ones people type. That was the cheap part, and it was overdue.

external.description:
Right after Meta Connect, Joanna Stern sat down with Mark Zuckerberg in Menlo Park and asked him about the new glasses, about Muse, and about the thing hanging over all of it: trust. I hadn't seen the interview yet, so I pressed record, watched it for the first time and paused whenever I had something to say. Which turned out to be quite often.

Here are the moments that stuck with me, and where I land on each.

### Trust is the issue Meta can't duck anymore

Zuckerberg opened on responsibility and labs taking their time, before anyone had asked about a product. That tells you something. People are afraid of what AI can do, and rightfully so. For most companies trust is one topic among many. For Meta it is the topic, and every launch now gets read through it.

His answer is that alignment, an AI system doing what you actually tell it to do, is the most important capability right now. More than getting better at math. I agree with the direction. Where I disagree is the implication that we're nearly there.

### An AI that keeps correcting itself is not a feature

Joanna mentioned that Muse keeps coming back to her with "you know what, I got something wrong." Zuckerberg called it reflective. I call it a problem. I see the same pattern with Claude's latest models: it keeps revising answers after the fact because it made mistakes the first time. In a chat that's charming. In an agent that books, buys and emails on your behalf, a correction after the fact is a cost that already happened.

> As Ethan Mollick puts it in _Co-Intelligence_ : hallucinations are a deep part of how LLMs work.

That's why the operator in the loop still matters. The people who get real leverage out of these tools are the ones who know what the right answer looks like before the agent hands them one. I wrote about that from a different angle when I tested one of my Claude skills against an agent without it: the tool is only as good as the judgement checking it.

### The hardware finally looks like something people want

The lineup now runs from Ray-Ban Meta Audio at $349 to a $1,299 pair of VR glasses. The audio glasses have no camera at all, which quietly addresses the privacy worry around filming people without them knowing. And Meta says the hearing enhancement turns them into an FDA-cleared, over-the-counter hearing aid.

That last one is the part I'd underline as a marketer. It is a different target group entirely. We're all getting older, our hearing isn't getting better, and a lot of people skip a hearing aid because it feels bulky or embarrassing. A normal, stylish pair of glasses removes that barrier. It's the same distribution lesson I wrote about with the Muse Charm: put the product where people already are, in a form they already accept.

### Muse is Gemini Spark and Claude Cowork for everyone else

Strip away the avatar and Muse does what Gemini Spark and Claude Cowork already do for people who are comfortable with technical tools. It gets access to your computer, your accounts, your email and your messages, and you give it a goal instead of a task. The difference is that Meta made it less codey and more consumer-friendly, and it went straight to the top of the App Store. I can absolutely see the appeal.

Zuckerberg's own examples were telling. Find the subscriptions I'm not using and cancel them. Get us a hiking permit. Watch me spar and send feedback between rounds. Give it the goal, and it goes and works on it. That's the endpoint we all want to reach. It's also exactly why the trust question matters so much more for an agent than for a chatbot. We already saw where the friction starts when Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site.

### Would you give it your Gmail?

Joanna hasn't connected her personal Gmail. She doesn't fully trust Meta with it, and she worries Muse might email people on her behalf in ways she didn't intend. Fair. My take is more pragmatic: if you don't want to share it, don't use it. If you have something to hide, also don't use it. But if you don't, the realistic worst case today is being offered a product at a good discount. We already hand this data to dozens of platforms.

Meta's answer is architecture. According to Zuckerberg, Muse runs in a confidential virtual machine that even Meta can't look into, with a separate sentinel agent that polices what goes in and out and asks you to confirm sensitive actions. He brought in Moxie Marlinspike, who helped build the encryption behind WhatsApp.

And here I think Meta gets too little credit. WhatsApp has had end-to-end encryption for everyone by default since 2016, across billions of users. That doesn't make every Meta product safe. It does mean the company has done this at scale before.

### AI and kids: time back, not time away

Joanna's biggest fear is kids growing up talking to an AI companion that agrees with them on everything. It's a real risk, and I'd add a marketing observation: a friendly little device like the Muse puck is destined to be used by kids, and engaging your future customers early is never an accident.

But Zuckerberg's baking example matched my own experience. Over the last twelve months, agents have taken over reports, finances and online orders for me. I catch myself opening certain tools less and less because the work simply runs. That time went back to my family. The same logic sits behind how a fractional executive works with a lean stack: less admin, more judgement.

### Where I land

Zuckerberg seems well aware of the current limits. It isn't done, not everything works the way it should, and the pace is still incredible. Meta finally has hardware people actually use and an agent that hit number one. If people come to trust these tools enough to say "find me the cheapest way from A to B, book it and send me the receipt," that changes how we live with technology.

Trust is the product now. The rest is features.
